1:
Why the priests are singled out when the whole people had sinned is answered the same way by two voices. Calvin grants they did not sin alone, but holds them first in wickedness because it was their office to correct what the people did amiss, their dissimulation encouraging the common people to sin. He puts the excuse in their own mouths, that the people are growing cold in God's worship and it is better imperfect sacrifices should be offered than none at all, and answers that their connivance was nothing but consent, since God promoted them to the priesthood for this very end, to preserve the worship of his name in integrity, and they knew of the prevailing profanations and held their peace. Henry traces the same line: the charges of the previous chapter fell on them as sacrificers, where they might plead that they only offered what the people brought, so here the corruption is traced to its source, their fault as teachers; had the priests given better instructions, the people would have brought better offerings. He adds that the governors of the churches are themselves under God's government.

What blessing it is that God threatens to curse is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch denies that the priests' revenues are meant, their tithes, atonement-money and portions of the sacrifices, and takes the blessings for those they pronounced upon the people by virtue of their office, which God will make ineffective or turn into their opposite; he notes that the verb is a perfect, affirming the curse has already taken effect, and the suffix distributive, of each particular blessing. Ellicott reports both readings without choosing, since the word is commonly used in the sense of a gift. Clarke takes it of temporal good simply, and remarks that when temporal blessings are not the means of leading us to God they will infallibly lead us to hell; he refers the curse already fallen to unfruitful seasons, and to a dearth which appears to have happened about this time.

The threat against the seed and the face is read carefully. Gill takes the seed for what they cast into the earth, and notes that the word may also mean rebuke. Clarke reports a rendering which makes the loss not of seed but of the shoulder, the part belonging to the priest, and glosses the second clause as God throwing their offerings back in their faces. Ellicott prefers to destroy for you the seed, meaning that of the crops, and recalls that because the people neglected the tithes the Levites were obliged to till the fields themselves. On the dung he supplies the point that gives the threat its edge: it is the dung of the festival sacrifices, which was to be carried outside the camp to an unclean place and burnt, so that priests who had profaned God's name by unfit offerings were to be treated in the most ignominious manner; and the last clause, by a Hebrew idiom, means they shall be carried away to it and treated like it. Wesley says the same more bluntly, that their most solemn days shall be as loathsome to God as dung, and they themselves fit for the dunghill.

On the covenant with Levi Ellicott makes his boldest suggestion. He would render the clause not that God's covenant might be with Levi but to be my covenant, so that this new decree, which God has been compelled to make against the house of Levi, stands as his covenant with him in place of the old one. Wesley reaches a milder form of it: if they will not keep the covenant of Levi among them, God will make it firm on his own part by punishing those who violate it. Henry answers how they shall know the message was sent: they shall know its original by its efficacy, and whence it comes by what it does.
5:
The covenant of life and peace is referred to three subjects. Gill denies that it was made with Aaron or Phinehas, or that temporal life and outward prosperity are meant, noting that Aaron lived a hundred and twenty-three years and that some Jewish writers give Phinehas above three hundred; he takes it for the covenant made with Christ from everlasting, of life because made with the Word of life, and of peace because the whole scheme of reconciliation was drawn in it. Clarke keeps the two terms but reads them evangelically: to man excluded from God's favour and sentenced to death, God gave a covenant sacrifice which secured life, both exemption from the death deserved and the inward life that issues in eternal life; and as it secured life so it gave peace, between God and man, between man and man, and between man and his conscience. Wesley takes the plain sense, of long and prosperous life assured to the Levites in their due ministrations. Ellicott would drop the preposition and render simply life and peace, meaning that by the covenant these were guaranteed to Levi, life in its highest sense and peace as the sum of blessing.

The clause about the fear draws Ellicott's closest work. He would first render it as fear, that is, as a motive for the fear of God; but he thinks a better reading makes God and Levi each perform his own part, God bestowing life and peace and Levi rendering fear, so that the verse should run: my covenant was with him, life and peace, and I gave them to him; fear, and he feared me, and trembled before my name.

The portrait of the faithful priest is broken into parts by Clarke, who counts six qualifications. Levi feared God and was a sincere worshipper, acting always as in the presence of a just and holy God; the law of truth was ever in his mouth, by which he directed his own conduct and that of others; he walked with God in peace, living so as to keep up union with him; and he turned many away from iniquity, becoming by upright administration and faithful exhortation the instrument of converting many sinners. This character, Clarke adds, suits every genuine minister of God. Wesley spreads the portrait over the whole line, naming Aaron, Eleazar and Phinehas and every priest or Levite of any age who feared God and was humble, and singling out that he judged neither with respect of persons nor for bribes. Ellicott sharpens two terms: the law of truth means right instruction in the law and judgment in accordance with it, the reverse being better called perversion than iniquity; and equity means integrity of life. On the last clause he quotes another writer, that here is a history of zeal for God's glory and of the conversion of sinners in men of whom the world knows nothing, and of whose working, but for these three words at the close of the Old Testament, we should have known nothing.

What the priest's lips are for divides them again. Gill carries the verse straight to Christ as the great High Priest, whose lips have kept knowledge in the sense of not concealing but preserving it and communicating it freely, first to his disciples and then to others. Ellicott stays with the priest and presses the verb, which is not to keep as in a repository but to observe, that is, to speak in accordance with the knowledge of God revealed in the law; and he notes that the word rendered messenger is literally angel. Wesley draws the practical distinction, that all God's people ought to know the law but the priest more than others. Keil and Delitzsch reads these two verses together as the depiction of the way the priests ought to have walked, and which the next verse charges them with leaving.
8:
The charge of having left the way is put by each voice at a different distance. Clarke states it in a line, that they are become impure themselves and have led others into iniquity. Gill takes the way for the way of truth and righteousness, of life and peace, and applies the charge to the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees of Christ's time, who not only failed in the matter of sacrifices complained of earlier but left the way of atonement those sacrifices pointed to, and led others out of it with them. Ellicott keeps the contrast with the preceding portrait, saying that the priests of the present day have done in every respect the reverse of what Levi did. He then presses the wording: the people are made to stumble not at the law but in it, since the priests gave false instruction in the law and allowed what it forbade, and so turned the law, which ought to have been a light to their feet and a lamp to their path, into a stumbling-block. Wesley says the same of their false expositions, that they violated the law, contradicted its great intentions, and did what in them lay to defeat them.

What follows is read by Ellicott as the exact reversal of the covenant. Because the priests have not kept God's ways, he is no longer bound by the covenant he made with the tribe of Levi, and instead of life and peace he gives them contempt. Gill fixes the fulfilment historically, in the destruction of the city and temple by the Romans and the captivity that followed, when the people became a taunt and a proverb in all places where they came. Clarke takes it as a standing rule rather than a single event: the people despised these priests because they saw them acting contrary to their own functions, and the same thing has happened repeatedly since to whole classes of clergy who, failing to maintain by purity of life and soundness of doctrine the dignity of the ministerial office, became contemptible before the people and had their meagre preaching disregarded.

The last charge, of partiality, is given a narrower sense than the English suggests. Ellicott takes being partial in the law to mean partiality in the administration of justice, and points out that the authority of the priests, the Levites and the judges in matters both ceremonial and civil was expressly established by the law itself, so that the fault lies not in their holding the office but in their handling of it; he notes that it was on the strength of that same standing authority that our Lord told the people the scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. Wesley gives the motive rather than the mechanism, that they perverted the law to please great men or to serve some unworthy design; and he turns the verse on his own readers, asking whether, when we inquire into the reasons for the contempt of the clergy, this ought to be forgotten.
10:
The one father of the opening question is identified four ways. Gill lays them side by side: Adam, of whose blood all nations are made; Abraham, of whom as their father the Jews used to glory; Jacob, as two Jewish commentators take it; or God, Father of all men by creation and of that nation by adoption. Ellicott decides for the last, since God is the spiritual Father of the nation and in him they are all brothers and sisters; on that footing marrying a heathen woman or divorcing an Israelite wife is an offence against God and a violation of the fraternal relation, and he adds that the nation was created to be a witness to God's unity, an object which idolatresses admitted into their families would be fatal to. Wesley keeps to Abraham or Jacob, with whom the covenant was made, and reads the creating as the gracious work by which they were made a chosen people.

Henry uses the verse to connect the two halves of the chapter. Corrupt practices, he says, are the genuine fruit of corrupt principles, and the badness of men's lives is owing to loose notions they govern themselves by; here are men dealing falsely with one another because they think falsely of their God, and he who is false to his God cannot be expected to be true to his friend. Having defrauded God in tithes and offerings, their conscience was debauched and its bonds broken, and a door opened to all manner of dishonesty. He weighs two identifications of the treachery, the extortion complained of in the same period and the marriage abuses alongside it, and prefers the second, finding two charges under it: taking strange wives of heathen nations, and putting away the wives they had of their own, the first in contempt of the covenant of peculiarity and the second of the marriage covenant. Clarke reads the scope the same way, and adds the causal link, that the divorces seem to have been multiplied for the very purpose of contracting the prohibited marriages.

What exactly was profaned is stated briefly. Ellicott takes the holiness of the Lord for their own holy nation, and the daughter of a strange god for a woman who worships one, such as they were forbidden to marry; Clarke says the same in a line. Wesley refers the clause about what God loved to Judah instead, and takes the daughters for idolatresses received by men who had wives already and now cast them off. Gill leaves the marriages altogether and refers Judah's treachery to the betrayal of Christ to the Gentiles.

The threatened cutting off turns on a phrase found nowhere else, and Ellicott refuses the traditional rendering. Master and scholar is the Talmudic interpretation, but he calls it unsuitable as well as philologically precarious, since the passage concerns the whole nation and not its appointed teachers. He would render watchman and answerer, the watchman who cried in the city, Who comes there, and the man who answers, Friend, an exhaustive expression for every living person and so for all posterity; and he supports it from an Arabic phrase in the life of Tamerlane, that when he left the city there was not a crier or an answerer in it. He notes that the Chaldee reaches the same sense by son and son's son, and that of three possible explanations of the closing clause he prefers the one making it a repetition in other terms, a descendant enjoying religious privileges. Clarke and Wesley keep the received words, Clarke applying them to the man who teaches such doctrine and the man who follows it, and Wesley making the threat that there shall be left neither any to teach nor any to learn. Gill takes the sentence as the destruction not of one man and his family but of the whole nation and its polity.
13:
The tears on the altar are agreed to be the wives' own. Ellicott says the prophet now turns from the foreign marriages to the frivolous divorces that were their natural result, and takes the weeping for the plaints of Israelitish women divorced against their will; on the opening words he allows they may mean this is a second thing you do, but thinks the received rendering, which the Hebrew accentuation supports, not improbably right, and reads it as doing the thing again after the abuse had been reformed and solemnly renounced. Clarke puts the scene concretely: the poor women, divorced by cruel husbands, come to the priests and appeal to God at the altar, and the priests do not speak against so glaring an injustice. Wesley has them flying to the temple to cry to God for redress.

On the question the offenders ask in reply, Gill reports a Jewish commentator who calls it an instance of their impudence. Ellicott hears supercilious surprise, and on the word witness recalls the old covenant sworn at Mizpah, adding that if people considered what that verse means they would not be so fond of putting the name on their rings, since it denotes a strong suspicion as to the other party's fidelity. Clarke turns the witness against the priests, who had witnessed the contract and then failed to execute the discipline of the law on the husband; and he states the practice bluntly, that they kept their wives till their youth was past and then put them away to get young ones in their place. Wesley presses the phrase about the covenant, that a man is so firmly bound to such a wife that while she continues faithful he cannot be loosed.

The next verse is obscure enough that the voices do not agree on its shape. Gill and Wesley read it as a question about the creation, whether God did not make one woman only and bring her to Adam, so that his will was that one man should have but one wife at a time. Clarke draws out the arithmetic: God had the residue of the Spirit and could have made millions of pairs, yet made one pair from whom all should proceed, so that children might be the marked property of one man and one woman. He adds that a godly seed may point to the Messiah, since had there been several heads of families in the beginning, Christ must have been incarnated from each to taste death for every man. Keil and Delitzsch reads the clause not as a question at all but as a flat statement, that no man who had still a remnant of spirit ever did such a thing.

Ellicott builds his own rendering on the same word, taking remnant as superiority, and asking whether any man has such superiority of spirit as would justify treating his wife as a mere slave and divorcing her against her will; he remarks that the passage stands nearer the spirit of the gospel on divorce than the older law. On the garment he gives two options, an Oriental way of speaking of the wife, or the outward symbol of the man's inner state; and the word rendered violence, he notes, is used especially of ill-treatment of a wife. Gill records a marginal rendering, followed by the Targum, turning the clause into a permission: if he hate her, put her away.

The closing charge of wearying God is softened and sharpened. Gill observes that it is said after the manner of men, weariness not being properly attributable to God. Clarke takes it as patience at an end, tracing the taunt to the delay of punishment. Ellicott marks a new section beginning here, against the people's discontent because the expected manifestation of God's glory did not come at once; since evildoers seem to flourish, they conclude that God delights in them.
